source_text: Καὶ εἰ μὲν δοκεῖ ὑμῖν λόγου καὶ ἀληθείας ἔχεσθαι, τιμήσατε αὐτά· εἰ δὲ λῆρος ὑμῖν δοκεῖ, ὡς ληρωδῶν πραγμάτων καταφρονήσατε, καὶ μὴ ὡς κατ᾿ ἐχθρῶν κατὰ τῶν μηδὲν ἀδικούντων θάνατον ὁρίζετε. Προλέγομεν γὰρ ὑμῖν, ὅτι οὐκ ἐκφεύξεσθε τὴν ἐσομένην τοῦ θεοῦ κρίσιν, ἐὰν ἐπιμένητε τῇ ἀδικίᾳ· καὶ ἡμεῖς ἐπιβοήσομεν· Ὃ φίλον τῷ θεῷ, τοῦτο γενέσθω! Καὶ ἐξ ἐπιστολῆς δὲ τοῦ μεγίστου καὶ ἐπιφανεστάτου Καίσαρος Ἀδριανοῦ, τοῦ πατρὸς ὑμῶν, ἔχοντες ἀπαιτεῖν ὑμᾶς καθὰ ἠξιώσαμεν κελεῦσαι τὰς κρίσεις γενέσθαι, οὐκ ἐκ τοῦ κεκρῖσθαι τοῦτο ὑπὸ Ἀδριανοῦ μᾶλλον ἠξιώσαμεν, ἀλλ᾿ ἐκ τοῦ ἐπίστασθαι δίκαια ἀξιοῦν τὴν προσφώνησιν καὶ ἐξήγησιν πεποιήμεθα. Ὑπετάξαμεν δὲ καὶ τῆς ἐπιστολῆς Ἀδριανοῦ τὸ ἀντίγραφον, ἵνα καὶ κατὰ τοῦτο ἀληθεύειν ἡμᾶς γνωρίζητε. Καὶ ἔστι τὸ ἀντίγραφον τοῦτο. Μινουκίῳ Φουνδανῷ. Ἐπιστολὴν ἐδεξάμην γραφεῖσάν μοι ἀπὸ Σερηνίου Γρανιανοῦ, λαμπροτάτου ἀνδρός, ὅντινα σὺ διεδέξω. Οὐ δοκεῖ οὖν μοι τὸ πρᾶγμα ἀζήτητον καταλιπεῖν, ἵνα μήτε οἱ ἄνθρωποι ταράττωνται καὶ τοῖς συκοφάνταις χορηγία κακουργίας παρασχεθῇ. Ἄν οὖν σαφῶς εἰς ταύτην τὴν ἀξίωσιν οἱ ἐπαρχιῶται δύνωνται διϊσχυρίζεσθαι κατὰ τῶν Χριστιανῶν, ὡς καὶ πρὸ βήματος ἀποκρίνεσθαι, ἐπὶ τοῦτο μόνον τραπῶσιν, ἀλλ οὐκ ἀξιώσεσιν οὐδὲ μόναις βοαῖς. Πολλῷ γὰρ μᾶλλον προσῆκεν, εἴ τις κατηγορεῖν βούλοιτο, τοῦτό σε διαγινώσκειν. Εἴ τις οὖν κατηγορεῖ καὶ δείκνυσί τι παρὰ τοὺς νόμους πράττοντας, οὕτως διόριζε κατὰ τὴν δύναμιν τοῦ ἁμαρτήματος· ὡς μὰ τὸν Ἡρακλέα, εἴ τις συκοφαντίας χάριν τοῦτο προτείνοι, διαλάμβανε ὑπὲρ τῆς δεινότητος καὶ φρόντιζε ὅπως ἂν ἐκδικήσειας.
pass_a_gloss: And if indeed it seems to you to have reason and truth, honor them; if however it seems to you to be nonsense, despise them as worthless matters, and do not ordain death for those who do no wrong, as for those who are enemies. For we say to you, that you will not escape the coming judgment of God, if you persist in unrighteousness; and we will cry out. What is dear to God, let it be! And we have also from the letter of the greatest and most illustrious Caesar Hadrian, your father, to demand from you as we have asked to command the judgments to be made, not because we asked for this to be decreed by Hadrian, but because we know that the petition and explanation are just. We have also submitted a copy of Hadrian's letter, so that you may know that we are telling the truth in this matter as well. And there is this copy. To Minucius Fundanus. I have received a letter written to me by Serenius Granianus, a most illustrious man, whom you have succeeded. It does not seem to me, therefore, to leave the matter unexamined, so that people may not be troubled and a handle for wickedness may not be given to informers. If, then, the provincials are able to make a strong case against the Christians, so as to answer even before a court, let them turn to this alone, and not make demands with mere shouts. For it is much more fitting, if someone wishes to accuse, for you to examine this. If someone, then, accuses and shows that they are doing something contrary to the laws, thus judge according to the power of the sin; but if someone brings this forward for the sake of slander, take care of the seriousness and consider how you may avenge.

choices.english: for those who do no wrong

pass_b_english: If it seems to you that our case possesses reason and truth, then honor them; but if it seems to you to be nonsense, despise these things as worthless, and do not ordain death for people who do no wrong, as though they were enemies. For we declare to you that you will not escape the coming judgment of God if you persist in unrighteousness, and we will cry out: Let what is dear to God come to pass! We also possess a letter from the greatest and most illustrious Caesar Hadrian, your father, which we cite to demand that you order the trials to proceed, just as we requested. We did not ask this because we wanted Hadrian to decree this specific outcome, but because we know the petition and the explanation are just, and we have made them. We have also submitted a copy of Hadrian's letter so that you may know we are telling the truth in this matter as well. Here is that copy: To Minucius Fundanus. I have received a letter written to me by Serenius Granianus, a most illustrious man, whom you have succeeded. It does not seem right to me, therefore, to leave the matter unexamined, lest people be troubled and an opportunity for wickedness be given to informers. If, then, the provincials are able to make a strong case against the Christians, so as to answer even before a tribunal, let them have recourse to this alone, and not rely on mere petitions or shouts. For it is far more fitting, if someone wishes to accuse, for you to examine the charge. If someone accuses and demonstrates that they are doing something contrary to the laws, then judge according to the severity of the offense; but by Hercules, if someone brings the charge for the sake of slander, take the seriousness to heart and see to it how you may exact vengeance.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text, including the conditional structures and the distinction between the legal petition and the emperor's decree. Pass B correctly handles the idiom 'ὡς μὰ τὸν Ἡρακλέα' (by Hercules) which Pass A omitted, and correctly translates 'δεινότητος' as 'severity/seriousness'.
